caption:
CVE-2026-53359 sat in Linux KVM's shadow paging code for sixteen years before anyone found it. It has since been dubbed Januscape.

Security researcher Hyunwoo Kim (@v4bel) traced it to a use-after-free: KVM reused an old shadow page without checking what type of page it actually was, then read from that page after it had already been freed. The bug has been there since commit 2032a93d66fa in August 2010 (kernel 2.6.36). It was fixed by commit 81ccda30b4e8, merged June 19, 2026.

Here is why it matters. A guest VM with root can corrupt host kernel memory. On a shared physical machine, that means one rented VM can potentially take down or compromise every other tenant on the same box, with no cooperation from QEMU or the hypervisor's userspace needed. Kim reported it to Google's kvmCTF as a zero-day (the program pays up to $250,000 for a full guest-to-host escape). His public proof-of-concept panics the host. He says a full host-code-execution exploit exists too. He has not released it.

It hits both Intel and AMD x86, and Kim says it is the first guest-to-host PoC that works on both. ARM64 is unaffected (that is a separate bug, ITScape). The catch: it needs nested virtualization exposed to the guest. On distros where /dev/kvm is world-writable by default, like RHEL, this also works as a plain local privilege escalation with no VM required.

Fixed stable versions shipped July 4, 2026: 7.1.3, 6.18.38, 6.12.95, 6.6.144, 6.1.177, 5.15.211, and 5.10.260. NVD has not assigned a CVSS score yet. Do not wait for one to patch. If you cannot patch today, disable nested virtualization for untrusted guests: kvm_intel.nested=0 or kvm_amd.nested=0.

The thesis is direct: a shared host is not a security boundary you can trust by default. It is exactly as strong as the kernel patching it, and that kernel just went 16 years with this hole open.

Would you know if your cloud provider had actually patched this yet? Tell me below.

Follow for real threats and real tools, no fake panic.

narration.text: A bug that has been hiding in Linux's virtualization code since 2010 finally got a name: Januscape.
It lets a rented virtual machine with root access corrupt the memory of the physical server underneath it.
Patches shipped July 4th for every major kernel branch, so update now instead of waiting on a CVSS score that has not landed.
A shared host is only as safe as the kernel patching it, and this one just spent sixteen years unpatched.
Check with your cloud provider before you assume they have already handled it, and follow for more of these breakdowns.
